meta.title: MAIA — Music Adversarial Inpainting
meta.description: MAIA research page: importance-driven music adversarial attacks, verified GACELA regeneration, paper evidence, and limitations.

hero.subtitle: Music Adversarial Inpainting Attack
hero.description: Locate influential musical regions, regenerate only those regions, and evaluate security impact together with perceptual quality.
hero.scope: Real GACELA output at fixed regions; no sample-level attack claim is inferred.

question.title: Can we induce an MIR model to misclassify by regenerating only the musical segments it relies on most?
question.body: Rather than dispersing dense additive perturbations across the waveform, MAIA first identifies the musical regions that contribute most to the model’s current decision. It then uses surrounding musical context to regenerate only those bounded regions, with guidance from the attack objective. The central question is whether this localized, model-aware generative intervention can achieve an effective attack while preserving musical coherence and perceptual quality.
question.localizeBody: Identify the time-frequency regions that contribute most to the target model’s current decision, using gradient-based analysis or query-based coarse-to-fine localization.
question.regenerateBody: Use a conditional music inpainting model to reconstruct only the selected regions from their surrounding context instead of perturbing the entire track.
question.evaluateBody: Reduce confidence in the correct class while jointly evaluating attack effectiveness, musical coherence and perceptual quality.

threat.title: Two access settings, one bounded-edit principle
threat.whiteBody: Grad-CAM localizes influential regions. Reconstruction and untargeted attack losses guide GACELA for at most 10 optimization iterations, with loss weights selected from {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}.
threat.blackBody: A 0.5-second coarse-to-fine masking procedure estimates region importance. CMA-ES then searches GACELA's latent space under a 1,000-query budget.
threat.scope: The paper evaluates cover-song identification with CoverHunter on SHS100K and music-genre classification with IDS-NMR on GTZAN.

rationale.title: Change less, but change what matters
rationale.body: MAIA does not edit the whole waveform. It first ranks influential regions, then constrains generative changes to a small set of selected intervals. This makes the intervention interpretable in time and gives the inpainting model surrounding context for musically plausible reconstruction.

method.title: How MAIA Works
method.subtitle: A three-step importance-driven adversarial inpainting framework
method.step1Body: Identify critical time-frequency regions that most influence the model's decision
method.schematicNote: Illustrative mechanism — not a measured sample
method.deepDiveTitle: Technical deep dive: How are the critical regions located?
method.deepDiveBody: Open either access setting when you want the computation, formula, and evidence boundary.
method.gradcam1Body: The waveform is converted into a time-frequency representation and passed through the target MIR model. Grad-CAM starts from the score of the model’s current class.
method.gradcam2Title: 2. Weight feature maps by class gradients
method.gradcam2Body: Gradients of the selected class score are propagated to the target convolutional layer. Spatially averaged gradients assign a class-specific importance weight to each feature-map channel.
method.gradcam3Title: 3. Map positive evidence back to the spectrogram
method.gradcam3Body: The weighted feature maps are aggregated and passed through ReLU. After normalization and coordinate mapping, high-intensity areas become candidate adversarial regions.
method.figure2Alt: Grad-CAM heatmap on a mel-spectrogram from the MAIA paper
method.gradcamBoundary: Grad-CAM is an existing localization method. MAIA’s contribution is not the invention of Grad-CAM, but its use within an importance-driven music inpainting attack pipeline.
method.coarse1Body: The audio is divided into non-overlapping coarse chunks. Each chunk is zero-masked in turn, with a short Tukey taper applied at its boundaries.
method.coarse2Title: 2. Query the model and rank the chunks
method.coarse2Body: A chunk is considered important when masking it produces a large change in the loss associated with the original label. Division by duration keeps scores comparable across different segment lengths.
method.coarse3Body: The highest-scoring segment is recursively subdivided and evaluated again. Refinement continues until the desired granularity is reached or the query budget is exhausted, after which the top-ranked regions are selected.
method.blackBoundary: This procedure does not require model parameters or gradients, but it does require prediction feedback from repeated model queries. The paper’s 1,000-query cap applies to the overall black-box attack, not to each localization round.
method.step2Body: Select the highest-ranked regions for bounded generative modification
method.priorityBody: Rank candidate regions by model-derived importance and retain the top regions under the edit budget.
method.refineBody: In the black-box setting, recursively split the highest-scoring coarse region to obtain finer localization.
method.step3Body: Reconstruct selected segments with GACELA and task-specific adversarial guidance
method.contextBody: GACELA does not generate an isolated segment from scratch. Its generator is conditioned on the audio surrounding the masked interval, allowing the regenerated gap to connect with the musical content before and after it. MAIA keeps the outside context unchanged and modifies only the selected region.
method.outsideUnchanged: Only the selected interval is replaced; audio outside the mask comes directly from the original input.
method.figure4BeforeAlt: Before inpainting, from the paper figure
method.figure4AfterAlt: After inpainting, from the paper figure
method.figure4Caption: The paper figure illustrates context-conditioned local music reconstruction.
method.whiteOptimizationTitle: White-box optimization: reconstruction, attack, and re-inpainting
method.whiteObjectiveAria: Joint white-box reconstruction and attack objective
method.recLossBody: Keeps the local reconstruction consistent with the musical context and perceptual quality.
method.attackLossBody: Reduces confidence in the original correct label y for an untargeted attack.
method.lambdaBody: Control the fidelity–attack trade-off; both are grid-searched over {0.5, 1.0, 2.0}.
method.iterationsBody: The white-box experiment performs at most 10 optimization iterations.
method.maskConstraint: The mask confines the update to the selected region.
method.whitePriorBoundary: The pretrained GACELA model is used as a generative prior. MAIA iteratively updates the selected audio region and re-projects it through the inpainting process; it does not jointly retrain GACELA with the target MIR model.
method.blackOptimizationTitle: Black-box optimization: latent-space search with CMA-ES
method.blackOpt1: Process candidate regions from highest to lowest importance.
method.blackOpt2: Sample latent candidates from the current CMA-ES distribution.
method.blackOpt3: Use GACELA to generate candidate fills under the same surrounding context.
method.blackOpt4: Query the target model for prediction-label or confidence feedback.
method.blackOpt5: Favor candidates that improve the attack objective and update the latent distribution.
method.blackOpt7: Stop after misclassification or when the overall query budget is exhausted.
method.whiteShortBody: Uses gradients to update the selected region.
method.blackShortBody: Uses model feedback to search the GACELA latent variable.
method.sharedShortBody: Both modify only localized regions and condition on the unchanged context.

demo.title: Real model-based regeneration at MAIA-selected regions
demo.disclaimer: This interactive example isolates the generative inpainting component of MAIA. The displayed audio is produced by an actual music inpainting model at the selected regions. Paper-level attack performance is reported separately and is not inferred from this individual example.
demo.locateBody: The highlighted centers preserve the three region positions used by the earlier MAIA page. They are provenance-preserved interface metadata, not a new target-model localization run.
demo.locateAlt: Original spectrogram with three selected regions
demo.regenerateBody: Each view uses the same 30-second time axis. GACELA's 32-frame checkpoint alignment is recorded in the manifest, and the original region centers are preserved.
demo.differenceAlt: Difference spectrogram calculated from the original and regenerated audio
demo.differenceCaption: Computed from the two WAV files. Changes outside the effective regions are zero in the validation output.
demo.listenBody: All three sources share one timeline. Switching tracks preserves the current position; region looping constrains playback to the selected interval.
demo.abToggleAria: Switch between original and regenerated audio at the same time
demo.regionAria: Choose a region for loop playback
demo.statusLoopOff: Region loop disabled; the whole excerpt will play.

evidence.title: Evidence and limitations
evidence.disclaimer: These values are aggregate results from Table 1 of the paper. They are not predictions or metrics for the interactive sample above.
evidence.tableCaption: Table 1 excerpt — MAIA rows reported for two tasks and two access settings
evidence.limit1Body: The paper studies two MIR tasks and two target system–dataset pairs; broader generalization requires additional targets and music domains.
evidence.limit2Body: White-box MAIA requires gradients and model access. Black-box MAIA relies on query feedback and uses up to 1,000 queries.
evidence.evaluation: The paper evaluates ASR, post-attack mAP or accuracy, FAD using MERT-V0, LSD, and a five-point subjective listening study with 100 participants.

robustness.title: Beyond attack success: transferability and transformation robustness
robustness.subtitle: Mechanism-based hypotheses and an evaluation roadmap—not additional results reported by the MAIA paper.
robustness.status: Not evaluated in the current paper
robustness.transferAdditive: Perturbations optimized for one source model may transfer when different models share similar decision boundaries, but transfer is not guaranteed.
robustness.transferMaia: MAIA’s localization and optimization are also source-model-aware. Local content-level regeneration may affect features shared by multiple models, but it may also overfit the source model’s important regions.
robustness.codecAdditive: Fine-grained, low-amplitude perturbations can be attenuated or distorted by MP3/AAC encoding, resampling, and bitrate changes.
robustness.codecMaia: Because MAIA replaces a local region with plausible generated musical content, its modification may be less dependent on exact waveform-level noise. This suggests possible persistence after transcoding, but it was not tested.
robustness.codecStatus: Hypothesis only—no codec-robustness result is reported.
robustness.denoiseAdditive: Noise-like components may be reduced by denoisers or frequency filtering, although adaptive attacks can be designed against a known defense.
robustness.denoiseMaia: Content-like inpainted segments may not be recognized as noise by a denoiser, but denoising can still alter generated details and reduce attack effectiveness.
robustness.temporalAdditive: Cropping, time shifting, resampling, loudness normalization, or playback-recording can disrupt perturbations that depend on precise alignment.
robustness.temporalMaia: MAIA modifies bounded musical content, but its importance mask and target-model effect may still depend on timing and alignment.
robustness.temporalStatus: Not established by the current experiments.
robustness.road1Body: Craft attacks on one MIR model and evaluate them directly on different architectures and training datasets without re-optimizing the adversarial sample.
robustness.road2Body: Evaluate MP3/AAC transcoding at multiple bitrates, resampling, denoising, filtering, loudness normalization, time shifting, and playback-recording transformations.
robustness.road3Body: Measure post-transformation attack success, confidence change, perceptual distance, and listening quality instead of reporting attack success alone.
robustness.conclusion: MAIA demonstrates a stronger attack–quality trade-off than the evaluated PGD, C&W, NES, and ZOO baselines in the paper’s original settings. Whether this advantage extends to cross-model transfer or real audio-processing pipelines remains an empirical question.

bridge.title: From Localized Music Attacks to Multimodal Agent Safety
bridge.subtitle: A methodological transfer, not an experimental result of MAIA.
bridge.a1: Identify high-risk observations, context, memory, or actions
bridge.a3: Perform gradient-based and query-based red teaming
bridge.m4: Measure attack effectiveness and perceptual quality together
bridge.a4: Evaluate security impact, task utility, side effects, and human perception
bridge.boundary: MAIA does not directly solve prompt injection, jailbreak, tool authorization, or trusted execution. The bridge identifies a transferable evaluation methodology: locate influential inputs, apply bounded counterfactual changes, and jointly measure attack effectiveness and utility preservation.
